healthcareSystem: Mixed public-private. Public hospitals are under-resourced. Private clinics in Guatemala City and Antigua offer better care. Very limited in rural and indigenous areas.
qualityNotes: Private hospitals in Guatemala City offer reasonable care. Antigua has some private clinics for tourists. Healthcare in rural areas and near Lake Atitlán is very basic. For serious emergencies, evacuation to Guatemala City or Mexico City may be needed.
pharmacyHours: Pharmacies open 8am-8pm. Carolina and Galenica chains have longer hours. Limited in rural areas.
pharmacyTips: Pharmacies in cities are reasonably stocked. Prices are low. Many medications available without prescription. Staff speak Spanish. Bring essential medications for rural travel around Lake Atitlán or Tikal.
prescriptionRules: Many medications available without strict prescription. Controlled substances require documentation.

restrictedMeds.name: Cannabis/CBD products
restrictedMeds.note: Illegal. Possession can result in arrest.

bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter listing medications. Spanish translation helpful. Keep medications in original packaging. Bring all essential medications from home.

travelInsurance.tips: Travel insurance with medical evacuation is essential. Tikal and Lake Atitlán are remote — evacuation to Guatemala City can be costly. Ensure coverage includes altitude sickness and adventure activities.

recommended: Malaria prophylaxis (for lowland areas including Petén/Tikal region)
vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations. Malaria risk in lowland areas (Petén, Atlantic coast) — prophylaxis recommended for Tikal visits. Dengue and Zika risk in lowlands. Altitude sickness possible at Lake Atitlán (1,560m) and higher areas.

waterNotes: Tap water is NOT safe to drink anywhere in Guatemala. Use bottled water for drinking and brushing teeth. Avoid ice outside of tourist restaurants.
foodSafetyTips: Eat at established restaurants, especially in Antigua and Guatemala City. Be cautious with street food. Avoid raw vegetables and unpeeled fruits. Food at tourist-oriented restaurants in Antigua is generally safe.
medicalTourismNote: Guatemala is not a major medical tourism destination. Some dental tourism exists in Guatemala City due to low costs.
metaDescription: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Guatemala. Emergency numbers, malaria prevention for Tikal, pharmacy tips, water safety, and medical evacuation insurance for Lake Atitlán.

hospitals.name: Hospital Herrera Llerandi
hospitals.notes: Leading private hospital. JCI-accredited. Some English-speaking staff.

hospitals.name: Centro Médico Militar
hospitals.notes: Well-equipped military hospital open to civilians. Good trauma care.

hospitals.name: Hospital Privado Hermano Pedro
hospitals.notes: Private hospital in the main tourist town. Basic but clean. Spanish only.

pharmacyPhrases.english: I need medicine for a headache
pharmacyPhrases.local: Necesito medicina para el dolor de cabeza

dentalCare.availability: Dental care available in Guatemala City and Antigua at very low costs.
dentalCare.costRange: Q100-300 ($13-39) for consultation; Q200-800 ($26-103) for procedures
dentalCare.notes: Low-cost dental care. Quality varies — use recommended clinics.
dentalCare.emergencyTip: Hospital Herrera Llerandi has dental services. Private dental clinics in Antigua.

mentalHealth.crisisLine: Not widely established — contact Hospital de Salud Mental Federico Mora
mentalHealth.englishTherapists: Very limited. Some English-speaking therapists in Antigua through expat community.
mentalHealth.notes: Mental health services are very limited. Antigua has some international-oriented therapists.

accessibilityInfo.overview: Accessibility is very limited. Cobblestone streets in Antigua, uneven terrain at ruins.
accessibilityInfo.hospitalAccess: Major hospitals in Guatemala City have basic accessibility.
accessibilityInfo.transport: No accessible public transport. Private drivers recommended.
accessibilityInfo.tips: Antigua's cobblestone streets are very challenging for wheelchairs. Tikal involves extensive walking on uneven ground. Lake Atitlán requires boat access with steep docks.

covidStatus.entryRequirements: No COVID testing or vaccination requirements.
covidStatus.testing: Available at private hospitals in Guatemala City.
covidStatus.notes: Waterborne diseases, dengue, and malaria (in Petén) are more relevant health concerns.

insuranceClaimProcess: Hospitals require upfront payment (cash preferred). Keep all receipts. Documentation primarily in Spanish. Major private hospitals can provide English summaries on request.
